title: Emergent frustrated magnetism in strain-patterned graphene
authors: Yu-Chiang Hsieh, Wen-Han Kao, Christophe De Beule, Sheng-Zhu Ho, Ru-Long Gou, Bo-Nian Chen, Kuan-Yu Chou, Kuo-En Chang, Chin-Chia Chang, Ying-Mei Yang, Ching-Hua Kao, Hao-Chien Chiang, Jyun-Lin Chen, Sheng-Chin Ho, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming-Hao Liu, Ching-Hao Chang, Yi-Chun Chen, Ying-Jer Kao, Tse-Ming Chen
abstract: Geometrically frustrated magnetism conventionally arises from pre-existing magnetic moments on lattices whose geometry prevents their interactions from being simultaneously satisfied, giving rise to highly degenerate states and rich collective behavior. Creating such frustration in an intrinsically non-magnetic material presents a fundamentally different challenge, requiring both the magnetism and the competing interactions to emerge from correlated electrons. Here we show that this can be realized in graphene through lithographically programmable strain engineering. Patterning strain and the associated pseudo-magnetic field (PMF) into superlattices creates a correlated electronic system with flat bands and strong interactions. Transport measurements reveal interaction-driven insulating behavior, anisotropic magnetic hysteresis, and slow relaxation dynamics reminiscent of spin freezing, qualitatively captured by Monte Carlo simulations of competing magnetic moments on the PMF-defined ruby superlattice. Cryogenic magnetic force microscopy further reveals magnetic textures associated with the PMF landscape. These observations demonstrate frustrated magnetism emerging from correlated electrons in otherwise non-magnetic graphene. Our results establish lithographic strain engineering as a general and scalable route to flat bands and correlated states in van der Waals materials, providing a versatile platform for programmable quantum matter.
summary: This paper reports the realization of emergent frustrated magnetism in non-magnetic graphene by applying lithographically controlled strain patterns. The strain creates a pseudo-magnetic field that induces strongly correlated electronic states, leading to magnetic behavior analogous to spin ice. This establishes strain engineering as a versatile, scalable method for creating programmable quantum matter.
main_problem: The research addresses the fundamental challenge of realizing and studying emergent frustrated magnetism within an intrinsically non-magnetic material.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that lithographically patterned strain in graphene can induce correlated electronic states exhibiting robust, emergent frustrated magnetism, establishing a scalable platform for programmable quantum matter.
method: The study combines advanced experimental techniques, including transport measurements and cryogenic magnetic force microscopy, with theoretical modeling using spin-ice-like effective Hamiltonians and Monte Carlo simulations.
model_or_system: The physical system is graphene patterned into a superlattice via strain engineering, which generates a pseudo-magnetic field (PMF). This PMF induces flat electronic bands and strong electron correlations, leading to magnetic frustration analogous to spin ice.
key_observables: Anisotropic magnetic hysteresis, slow relaxation dynamics, insulating behavior characterized by Efros–Shklovskii variable-range hopping (ES-VRH), and spatially complex magnetic textures observed via MFM.
important_parameters: The effective magnetic moment ($\mu_{eff} \approx 9.0 \mu_B$), the critical magnetic fields ($H_{c,1}, H_{c,2}$) governing charge ordering phases, and the bandwidth of the induced flat bands ($< 6$ meV).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the strain patterning is perfectly programmable via lithography, and the magnetic response can be effectively modeled using spin-ice-like constraints derived from the PMF landscape.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device structure and PMF profiles, temperature-dependent resistivity showing insulating behavior, magnetotransport hysteresis loops, and MFM images confirming field-dependent magnetic textures.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform (strain-patterned graphene) to characterizing the electronic state (flat bands, correlated regime) via transport measurements, and finally modeling the emergent magnetic behavior using spin-ice analogies and simulating field-dependent charge ordering.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, tunable solid-state platform (graphene) to engineer complex quantum magnetic interactions, which is highly relevant for simulating exotic quantum phases without relying on rare magnetic elements.
